Procedures and conditions for LH dumping in flight are also 2 not yet in place. If in-flight dumping is allowed in the future, the LH would likely be vaporized 2 upon release such that there would be no evidence of the release from the ground below. Jet fuel vaporization is standard practice when conventional aircraft perform dumping in flight (Massey 2019). With LH flight, aircraft operators must also be aware of any boil-off gas that 2 accumulates in the onboard storage tank of the aircraft and know what measures can be taken to reduce pressure buildup in the storage tanks. Each of the items discussed here, as well as others not explored in this report, must be addressed with standardized procedures or regulations before LH -powered aircraft are commercialized. 2 4.3.2 Liquefied Natural Gas As an aviation fuel, the use of LNG is a significant departure from conventional jet fuel operations into the cryogenic handling of fuels like LH . LNG is stored at −162°C (111 K), 2 requiring well-insulated tanks, vapor management systems, and boil-off gas recovery. At the airport level, this would involve off-airport pipeline or tanker delivery to on-site cryogenic storage, with distributed refueling via cryogenic fuel trucks or potentially fixed cryogenic pipelines to gates. This contrasts with jet fuel’s relatively straightforward pumping; LNG handling relies on controlled pressure/temperature management to avoid rapid vaporization. 79 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Safety regulations for LNG are governed by a comprehensive framework of international, national, and industry-specific codes that collectively ensure safe production, storage, transportation, and refueling. The NFPA 59A (NFPA 2026b) is the principal U.S. standard regulating LNG facility design, construction, operations, and emergency response. It prescribes requirements for tank containment systems, minimum separation distances, spill containment, fire protection, and vapor cloud hazard mitigation based on decades of full-scale LNG safety research. Complementing NFPA 59A are other U.S. standards such as NFPA 52 (NFPA 2026c), which governs LNG and compressed natural gas fueling systems and is highly relevant for airports that may rely on LNG tanker trucks or mobile cryogenic refuelers. Internationally, LNG refueling and small-scale distribution systems are primarily governed by ISO 16924 (ISO 2026), which provides requirements for LNG fueling station design, operations, ventilation, hazardous zoning, and emergency shutdown systems. These ISO codes are widely used in Europe and Asia and form the backbone of global LNG refueling safety practices, many of which could be directly applicable to future airport LNG systems. The ISO 20519 standard specifies safety and operational requirements for bunkering of LNG for ships powered by LNG, including procedures, equipment, and risk management for safe fuel transfer operations (ISO 2021). The ISO 28460 standard provides guidelines for the ship to shore LNG transfer at ports, compatibility, and safety measures between LNG carriers and terminal facilities.
